A three-branch representation combines positive events, negative events, and recent-event timing through cross-branch attention and gating, followed by spatiotemporal aggregation. An ordered semantic-point head estimates relative correspondence precision for geometrically constrained pose recovery. Event-edge and CAD-projection agreement then guide local pose refinement under keypoint-geometry safeguards. At the sequence level, a ten-dimensional descriptor combines heatmap shape, reprojection consistency, and geometric conditioning to set time-aligned observation scales. On the official SPADES challenge test set, the complete system achieves a combined pose score of 0.0474, approximately 5.4\% below PASAN+IRIS. Validation ablations reduce the score from 0.0772 for base localization with uniform PnP to 0.0514 for the complete cascade; on identical single-frame observations, quality weighting reduces the score from 0.0549 with constant-weight optimization to 0.0514.

title: Axiomatic Learning and Probabilistic Structures with first applications to variants of Arithmetic Machine Learning and beyond
abstract: We introduce the Axiomatic Learning Structures (ALS) and Axiomatic Probabilistic Structure (APS) in order to study the interactions of Machine Learning, Optimization, with research frameworks- which, we take the view, can be characterized at the core by the corresponding axioms. The ALS explores the interplays between structures that one is interested in Learning Theory such as Loss functions and the axioms of the objects and transformations involved in these functions. The APS studies the interaction between structures of interest in Probability Theory such as Gibbs distributions, equations with noise, etc. and the axioms of the corresponding objects and transformations. We also introduce in Section 6 Transformations-Axiomatic Based Learning (TABLe) on Mathematical data-sets. One feature of this approach is the ranking of transformations from a table for a certain task based on scores which reflect which transformations work better than others, similarly to when human investigators try various methods on a task. We also study structure recovery from noisy data. In particular, to exemplify the ideas, we consider loss functions which contain derivations and derivations-like transformations. As a first application we study recovery in the context of polynomials with integer coefficients using standard derivatives along with other types of derivations which appear in Arithmetic: the p-derivations which satisfy \textit{different axioms} from the usual derivatives. As a first application of the APS we study a class of noisy (partial/mixed) derivations equations. In the last sections, to provide further potential applications of this framework, we give an overview of an initial simplified Opinion Dynamics model and its (simultaneous) study of rules of updates.

title: A Fibrational Framework For Multi-Conclusion Logics
abstract: The fibrational framework of Licata, Shulman, and Riley gives a uniform account of substructural and modal logics for single-conclusion judgments. This thesis extends it to a multiple-output setting in which cartesian resources may be used freely, while linear resources occur exactly once on either side of the turnstile. Judgments are indexed by descriptors: directed acyclic graphs generalizing the tree-shaped expressions of the original framework. Descriptor $2$-cells encode structural transformations, and explicit gates provide weakening, contraction, coweakening, and cocontraction at linear modes. We define a sequent calculus generated by two connectives, $F$ and $U$. We prove identity, invertibility, and cut admissibility. The mode and type theories present linear-non-linear $2$-polycategories, and the projection is a local discrete fibration and a fibration, with opcartesian lifts for one-output base morphisms. Two adequacy results validate the framework: its cartesian fragment recovers the Licata--Shulman--Riley calculus, and its purely linear fragment presents classical multiplicative linear logic. Finally, we relate indexed and fibrational semantics. After developing representability correspondences for multicategories and polycategories, we establish an equivalence between multi-indexed categories over a fixed representable base and multicategorical opfibrations over it, together with its biclosed bifibrational version. We also give a one-way construction from planar poly-indexed data to a planar polycategory.

title: Anomalous Structures of Fisher Zero Lines in Biorthogonal Dynamical Quantum Phase Transitions
abstract: Fisher zero lines of the Loschmidt amplitude in non-Hermitian quenches can exhibit anomalous structures in the complex time plane, such as divergence, separation, and the restriction of all branches or a specific branch to the real or imaginary axis. Here, we use the biorthogonal framework to reveal the origin of these structures and determine the corresponding critical momentum conditions by analyzing the values of $m_k=\hat{\mathbf{h}}_0\cdot\hat{\mathbf{h}}_1$, the dot product between the normalized prequench and postquench complex Bloch vectors. When Fisher zeros continuously cover the real-time axis, the density of Fisher zeros is further introduced to identify the critical times within these critical regions, at which the rate function becomes nonanalytic. We verify our results in a generalized non-Hermitian SSH model by quenching the Peierls phase and the non-Hermitian gain-loss strength, and also use the Jordan form to analyze the dynamics at postquench exceptional points, where the conventional Fisher zero formula is not applicable.

title: ASKAP Discovery of a Giant Odd Radio Circle at $z=0.15$
abstract: Odd radio circles (ORCs) are a recently recognized class of faint, roughly circular diffuse radio sources, typically a few hundred kiloparsecs across, whose origin is still debated. We report the serendipitous discovery of a giant ORC, ORC~J1928$-$5056, in 856~MHz continuum data from the ASKAP observations. The emission forms a single, mildly elliptical structure $4^{\prime}$ across, corresponding to $0.63$~Mpc at the redshift $z=0.1507$ of the central galaxy LEDA~140850, the brightest cluster galaxy of Abell~3639, which makes it one of the largest single ORCs known. After subtracting the radio nucleus associated with the host galaxy, the ORC has a flux density of 73~mJy integrated within an area of $\sim 12$~arcmin$^2$, i.e.\ a mean surface brightness of only $1.7$~$μ$Jy~arcsec$^{-2}$, and a rest-frame luminosity of $L_{1.4}=2\times10^{24}$~W~Hz$^{-1}$, comparable to those of the most luminous ORCs. Including its nucleus, the system reaches $L_{1.4}=6.6\times10^{24}$~W~Hz$^{-1}$, higher than that of any other ORC reported so far. The host is a massive ($M_{\ast}\sim10^{11}\,M_{\odot}$), passive elliptical galaxy with negligible star formation. It contains an AGN jet with a power-law spectrum of index $α=-0.877\pm0.089$ between 856 and 1656~MHz. Finally, we discuss the implications for ORC formation models and the observations needed to establish the nature of this system.

title: Cross-Day Compatibility of Daily Item Embeddings: An Empirical Study of Alignment, Scale Management, and CTR Adaptation
abstract: Daily item co-occurrence embeddings are paired with next-day behavior without future-behavior leakage. Multi-day click-through rate (CTR) training therefore mixes versions whose directions and norms may differ for the same item. We compare Word2Vec and an item-graph XSimGCL adaptation across initialization, inheritance, post-processing, training constraints, and downstream augmentation. The inventory contains 48 configurations, including 32 common-protocol CTR evaluations. Observed metrics are reported as relative percentage changes from the corresponding Word2Vec baseline (0%), with raw values and exact dataset sizes withheld. Three findings emerge. First, multiple upstream interventions improve compatibility and CTR. ID-init and orthogonal alignment increase cosine by 51.2% and 93.4%, and GAUC by 2.2% and 2.6%, relative to ordinary Word2Vec. Retrieval and geometry remain insufficient downstream surrogates. Second, warm starts perform strongly but accumulate scale. The day-matched norm increase over Word2Vec reaches 102.5% after eight days; daily global rescaling limits it to 8.2% and attains the highest observed GAUC increase, 4.0%. Third, CTR learning through a dimensionality-reducing encoder further adapts to residual drift. Against dimension-matched random-projection, SVD, and untrained-network controls, trained encoders attain the highest cross-day cosine for four of six upstream methods. The other two rank third and second in train-to-test cosine. These industrial results support complementary roles for upstream stabilization, inherited-scale management, and downstream task learning.

title: Stripe antiferromagnetic order and spin dynamics in the Shastry-Sutherland Ising compound Er2Be2GeO7
abstract: In rare-earth compounds, the interplay between geometric frustration and unusual single-ion anisotropy caused by the crystal electric field often leads to exotic magnetic phases. Here, we investigate the magnetic properties of the rare-earth Shastry-Sutherland compound Er$_2$Be$_2$GeO$_7$ using bulk measurements and neutron scattering down to sub-Kelvin temperatures. A $k=(0,0,0)$ stripe-like antiferromagnetic order with locally tilted Er$^{3+}$ moments is revealed by time-of-flight neutron powder diffraction, accompanied with a $λ$-shape specific-heat anomaly at $T_N=0.84$ K. The temperature dependence of the magnetic peak intensity corresponding to the ordered moment of Er$^{3+}$ approximates to the two-dimensional Ising universality class. Thermal- and cold-neutron inelastic scattering experiments demonstrate that the strong Ising anisotropy originates from the local crystal electric field, and reveal gapped magnetic excitations with weak dispersion in the ordered state. Mean-field random-phase approximation with inequivalent nearest-neighbor couplings accounts well for the collective excitations, while classical Monte Carlo simulations yield the fractional $1/4$ and $1/2$ magnetization plateaus. Our work provides a comprehensive description of the spin correlations in Er$_2$Be$_2$GeO$_7$ with a particular focus on the classical origin of its fractional magnetization plateaus.

title: A fully articulated humanoid dexterous hand with human-level joint structure enabled by linkage-based actuation
abstract: Humanoid dexterous hands are a core component of embodied intelligence, enabling robots to translate high-level intent into rich and adaptive physical interaction. However, existing designs remain constrained by a persistent trade-off among anthropomorphic kinematic complexity, mechanical robustness, load capacity and control simplicity, limiting dexterous manipulation in unstructured environments. Here we present Torch-Hand, a fully articulated humanoid dexterous hand that replicates the joint structure and motion hierarchy of the human hand with 21 degrees of freedom (DOF), comprising a highly articulated five-DOF thumb and four DOF in each of the remaining fingers. The differentiated thumb integrates multi-axis CMC motion to provide broad opposition and flexible contact orientation relative to the four fingers. Unlike tendon-driven or hybrid actuation approaches, Torch-Hand adopts an entirely linkage-based transmission architecture. By integrating screw-linkage actuation, the hand achieves high grasping force and substantial payload capacity while maintaining a compact anthropomorphic form. Its actuation architecture is optimized for control tractability, with all actuators integrated within the palm and arranged in a serial-robot-like configuration that establishes a direct correspondence between motor motion and joint kinematics. This architecture mechanically decouples functional DOF to reduce unintended inter-joint motion propagation, while allowing independently addressable DOF to be actively coordinated into coupled multi-joint motion patterns during complex manipulation. Comprehensive experiments assess reachable workspace, coordinated fingertip trajectories, thumb opposition, 33-grasp taxonomy coverage, grasping force, payload capacity and task-level manipulation. These results establish Torch-Hand as a robust hardware foundation for dexterous embodied manipulation.

title: OmniGlimpse: Asymmetric Identity Memory for Online Multi-View Tracking
abstract: Multi-view tracking extends visual coverage beyond a single camera, providing complementary observations when targets are occluded or leave the view. This raises a question: how can observations from different views be matched to the correct identities without offline scene-specific training or camera calibration? Progress toward this goal remains limited because many offline formulations assume such deployment-specific knowledge, while online adaptation can amplify association errors. We study this problem as online multi-view identity maintenance (OMIM): targets are initialized once per view, with no further identity labels provided after each initialization. To this end, we introduce OmniGlimpse, an asymmetric propose-verify framework that separates adaptive association from stable identity consolidation. At the representation level, short-term local and cross-view evidence is mapped into target-specific adaptive spaces to propose associations, whereas long-term identity distributions are maintained for verification in a canonical space defined by a frozen encoder. At the update level, short-term evidence may guide current associations, whereas, after bootstrapping, only verified observations may update persistent memory or drive adaptation. Under a unified target-specified evaluation protocol, OmniGlimpse improves over the best evaluated online baseline for each metric by 9.1 IDF1 and 22.1 CVIDF1 points on M3Track. The corresponding gains on MvMHAT are 20.3 and 26.2 points. Despite using no offline scene-specific training, it outperforms offline-trained references in IDF1 and remains competitive in cross-view association. These results support an approach to online identity maintenance that adapts to changing appearances while consolidating reliable evidence into stable identity anchors.

title: Brownian covariances on an interval: a complete endpoint classification
abstract: Brownian motion and the Brownian bridge have covariance kernels that are Green's functions of the negative second derivative on the unit interval, with mixed Dirichlet-Neumann and Dirichlet boundary conditions, respectively. We characterize the Green's functions of all strictly positive real self-adjoint realizations of this operator. The kernels are in one-to-one correspondence with positive-semidefinite $2\times2$ endpoint covariance matrices. We call the associated centered Gaussian processes Brownian processes. Each is a standard Brownian bridge plus the affine interpolation of an independent Gaussian endpoint vector. Singular endpoint covariance matrices give hard endpoint constraints, such as the pinned start $X(0)=0$ of Brownian motion. This parametrization gives explicit operator domains and energy spaces. On every mesh it gives an exact sparse precision matrix, so the likelihood of $n$ observations can be evaluated in $O(n)$ operations. Nonnegative realizations with a null space are treated separately through orthogonally normalized pseudoinverses, which are proper Gaussian covariances.

title: Orlicz-Sobolev with Musielak: An Efficient Regularization Approach for Graph-based IPM
abstract: We study the Sobolev IPM problem for probability measures supported on a graph metric space, where critic function is constrained to lie within the unit ball defined by Sobolev norm. Sobolev IPM is intrinsically coupled with $L^p$ geometric structure within its definition, limiting its ability to incorporate other prior geometry beyond the $L^p$ paradigm. Conversely, the classic optimal transport is flexible, easy to adapt to various geometric structures by simply changing its ground cost. An important example is Orlicz-Wasserstein (OW) which utilizes \emph{Orlicz} geometric structure to generalize the $L^p$ within the standard $p$-order Wasserstein, and remarkably play a vital role to advance machine learning methodologies. Inspired by recent advantages of OW, in this work, we leverage a specific class of convex functions for Orlicz geometry to mitigate such limitation for Sobolev IPM, and propose the generalized Sobolev IPM (GSI). Our GSI approach encompasses Sobolev IPM as a special case while accommodating diverse geometric priors beyond $L^p$. It however brings up significant computational hurdles that compound those already notoriously inherent in Sobolev IPM. To address these challenges, we theoretically establish a novel connection between \emph{Orlicz-Sobolev} norm and \emph{Musielak} norm which facilitates a novel efficient regularization for GSI. By further exploiting the underlying graph structure, we show that the regularized GSI reduces to a simple univariate optimization problem, achieving notably computational efficiency, enabling its usage in practical applications. We empirically illustrate that the regularized GSI is several-order faster than the popular OW in computation, and its performances compare favorably to other transport baselines for comparing graph-based measures in document classification and topological data analysis.

title: Automaton-based Characterisations of First Order Logic over Infinite Trees
abstract: We study the expressive power of First-Order Logic (\FO) over (unordered) infinite trees, with the aim of identifying robust characterisations in terms of branching-time specification formalisms. While such correspondences are well understood in the linear-time setting, the branching-time case presents well-known structural challenges. To this end, we introduce two classes of hesitant tree automata and show that they capture precisely the expressive power of two branching-time temporal logics, namely \PolPCTL and \CTLsf, both of which have been previously shown to be equivalent to \FO over infinite trees. These results provide uniform automata-theoretic characterisations and yield a natural normal form for the latter in terms of a new fragment of \CTLs called \PolCTLs. As a consequence, we identify a fundamental limitation of \FO in this setting: along each branch, it can express only properties that are either safety or co-safety, thereby revealing a sharp expressive boundary for first-order definability over infinite trees.

title: Characterization of Fourier transform of Hilbert space Valued functions
abstract: The aim of this paper is to obtain the characterization of Fourier transform for functions taking values in a separable Hilbert space $H$, defined on the groups $G=\R^n,\,G=\Z/n\Z$. In the first part of the paper, we consider the Fourier transform as a bijective mapping on $S_H$, the space of all $H$-valued smooth rapidly decaying functions on $\R^n$, which naturally extends bijectively to the dual space $S_H'$. Within this framework, we characterize the Fourier transform in terms of the convolution theorem, supplemented by additional structural properties of the Fourier transform. In the second part of the paper, we consider the discrete setting, where the Fourier transform is an operator on $L^1(\Z/n\Z, H)$, and we provide corresponding characterization based on its essential properties. In contrast to the classical setting, a key assumption in our framework involves the interplay between two distinct convolution operations. As a consequence, the structure of our proof diverges notably from the classical case and introduces additional complexities.

title: Wilson Towers as Local Bulk Fields
abstract: Multi-winding Wilson loops (Wilson spools) in 2+1-dimensional gravity can reproduce one-loop partition functions of local free fields in the bulk. Bulk free fields have a second-quantized Fock space, and the AdS/CFT correspondence suggests that the associated multi-particle sectors are dual to multi-trace primaries in the CFT. In this note, we use standard symmetric-function methods to show that the Wilson spool in thermal AdS$_3$ can be recast as a sum over $single$-winding Wilson loops -- one for each multi-trace primary. In a companion paper to appear, we will view Wilson networks and TQFTs as the natural language of non-perturbative bulk quantum gravity. The present note illustrates how this can apply to $local$ bulk fields, and not just defects: a bulk (generalized free) field is to be viewed as a full tower of multi-trace Wilson lines. We further show that the $SL(2)$ descendants of each multi-trace primary, together with the boundary gravitons of the AdS$_3$ background, correctly reproduce the full Virasoro character of each module. In this language, the role of a light insertion on a heavy primary is played by a topological Verlinde line. This allows us to obtain a "microscopic" description of one-loop determinants on the smooth BTZ handlebody. A spatially wound probe Wilson line on a torus with a contractible $thermal$ cycle can be traded for a Verlinde line inserted on a dense family of heavy Polyakov loops -- with the roles of the two cycles exchanged, so that the $spatial$ cycle is now contractible. The vacuum row of the modular $S$-kernel acts as the (approximate) density of the heavy primaries. This reinforces the case made in arXiv:2601.18775 that a smooth horizon is a stand-in for an ensemble of quantum states, each produced by a heavy Wilson line that appears as a singular horizon in the semi-classical limit.

title: The QCD phase diagram for three-flavor Möbius domain-wall fermions
abstract: We investigate the phase transition of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) with three degenerate quark flavors at zero baryon chemical potential. Using Möbius domain-wall fermions as the lattice fermion formulation, we ensure excellent chiral symmetry preservation. Our simulations are performed at three different temporal lattice extents, $N_{t}=6, 8, 12$, with a fixed lattice spacing $a=0.1361(20)$ fm, corresponding to temperatures of 242(4), 181(3), and 121(2) MeV, respectively. We explore a range of quark masses and spatial volumes with aspect ratios $N_{s}/N_{t}$ spanning from 2 to 4. By analyzing the mass and volume dependencies of the plaquette, plaquette susceptibility, chiral condensate, chiral susceptibilities, and Binder cumulant, we identify the pseudocritical transition quark masses from our largest lattice volumes. For $N_t=6$, this is 184(10) MeV (determined from the plaquette susceptibility). For $N_t=8$ and 12, the transition points vary slightly depending on whether the total or disconnected chiral susceptibility is used, yielding ranges of 36(1)-39.1(9) MeV and 3.5(3)-3.7(2) MeV, respectively, in the $\overline{\text{MS}}$ scheme at a scale of $μ=2$ GeV. The negligible volume dependence at $N_t=6$ and 8, combined with finite-size scaling analysis at $N_t=12$ revealing volume growth significantly weaker than expected for a first- or second-order phase transition, points to a continuous crossover at these specific quark mass points. Additionally, we study the effects of residual chiral symmetry breaking on the chiral condensate and chiral susceptibilities using two different values of $L_s$.

title: DIP-CAD: A Design-Intent-Preserving Agent Harness for Parametric CAD Modeling
abstract: Parametric CAD modeling requires not only matching the target shape, but also preserving design intent under parameter edits. However, most existing methods focus on improving static shape generation accuracy, while the dependencies that govern later edits are often overlooked. To tackle this issue, we present DIP-CAD, a design-intent-preserving agent harness for generating parametric CAD models from images. DIP-CAD combines vision-language model reasoning with CAD kernel operations to establish dependencies that encode the design intent. In parametric CAD, these dependencies are mainly established through geometry references in modeling commands and constraints in parametric sketches. At the command level, ID-based explicit geometry reference binds modeling commands to selected faces, edges, or vertices. At the sketch level, a local-coordinate bridge ensures accurate sketch placement, providing the basis for correctly establishing sketch constraints. Constraints among sketch primitives and constraints to external projected geometry further preserve both internal sketch relationships and dependencies on existing geometry. To provide a more comprehensive data foundation for parametric CAD modeling tasks, we introduce the Geometry Explicit Reference Dataset (GERD), whose structured data format links stepwise modeling commands to intermediate CAD models through explicit geometry references. On GERD-EVL and a DeepCAD test subset, DIP-CAD improves mIoU for static model generation by 11.1% and 5.6%, respectively. In parameter-editing evaluations, the corresponding mIoU improvements are 7.0% and 4.2%. Case studies further demonstrate how parameter edits drive shape updates while preserving design intent.

title: Quantum features of a non-commutative Schwarzschild black hole
abstract: This work aims to present some quantum aspects of a non-commutative (NC) gauge gravity formulation of a Schwarzschild-like black hole constructed via the Moyal twist $\partial_t \wedge \partial_θ$. Particle creation is estimated for bosonic and fermionic fields using the quantum tunneling method, with divergent integrals treated through the residue prescription. Since the surface gravity is well defined for this configuration, the corresponding emission rates and evaporation lifetimes are also computed. In addition, previously reported results in the literature on gauge gravity Schwarzschild black holes are revisited. Finally, we infer constraints on the NC parameter $Θ$ from solar system tests.

title: Wavefront sets for genuine representations of $\rm GL$-covers of Kazhdan--Patterson or Savin types
abstract: First, we consider general Brylinski--Deligne covers of the $p$-adic general linear groups, and discuss the theory of Bernstein--Zelevinsky derivatives. We also recall the Zelevinsky-type classification of the irreducible genuine spectrum for the Kazhdan--Patterson and Savin covers. Following this, for these two special families of covers, we determine the wavefront sets of their irreducible genuine representations, expressed in terms of the iterated degrees of the highest Bernstein--Zelevinsky derivatives. Finally, for Kazhdan--Patterson covers, we reinterpret this result on the wavefront set using a version of the local Langlands correspondence and the covering Barbasch--Vogan duality.

title: Counting Clues: A Lightweight Probabilistic Baseline Can Match an LLM
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel on multiple-choice clinical diagnosis benchmarks, yet it is unclear how much of this performance reflects underlying probabilistic reasoning. We study this through questions from MedQA that ask for the most likely diagnosis. We introduce Frequency-Based Probabilistic Ranker (FBPR), a lightweight method that scores options with a smoothed Naive Bayes over concept-diagnosis co-occurrence statistics from a large corpus. When co-occurrence statistics are sourced from Dolma, the pretraining corpus for OLMo, and RedPajama, an open reproduction of the LLaMA pretraining-data recipe, FBPR achieves comparable performance to the corresponding LLMs. Furthermore, direct LLM inference and FBPR exhibit complementary strengths, correctly answering largely different subsets of questions with overlap barely above chance. Combining them with a simple hybrid method yields a notable gain over either method alone. These findings show that explicit probabilistic baselines can account for a substantial portion of the benchmark performance on diagnosis questions, while serving as historically grounded reference points and complementary signals for hybridization.

title: A First-Step Bias Restores Lost Diversity in Diffusion Model Distillation
abstract: Distribution-matching distillation enables high-quality image generation in only a few denoising steps. However, distilled student models often map different initial noise samples to similar outputs under the same prompt. To locate where diversity is lost, we compare the teacher and student along the sampling trajectory. The largest measured reduction in the response to different initial noises occurs during the first, high-noise step. When we replace the first step with the teacher's corresponding trajectory and leave the final three student steps unchanged, most of the output diversity returns. This suggests that the first step is a key point for restoring diversity. Motivated by this finding, we introduce \emph{ReSeed}, a post-distillation method that adds a seed-response bias adapter only to the first student step and aligns its velocity with the teacher's first-interval secant velocity. All student weights and later denoising steps remain unchanged. We evaluate ReSeed on three text-to-image models (SD3-Medium, SD3.5-Medium, and FLUX.1-dev) and one text-to-video model (Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B). For a distilled 4-step FLUX.1-dev model, \emph{ReSeed} requires only $0.00196\%$ additional trainable parameters relative to the base model and is trained on 8,000 prompt--noise pairs, while keeping the distilled student fully frozen and requiring no target images, perceptual losses, or adversarial losses. It improves DINO diversity by $48.3\%$ while maintaining competitive visual quality. These results show that substantial diversity can be recovered through a lightweight, data-efficient tuning of only the first denoising step, without finetuning the full student model.

title: Sharp global \(L^2\) estimates for oscillatory integral operators with quasi-homogeneous phases
abstract: For one-dimensional oscillatory integral operators with real-analytic phases, the seminal work of Phong and Stein established that the Newton polygon of the mixed Hessian of the phase determines the sharp local \(L^2\)-decay. The local theory relies on spatial localization near the origin and therefore does not capture the global geometry of the real zero set of the Hessian. For globally defined operators, unbounded real zero curves of the Hessian can make the global decay strictly slower than the local decay or destroy \(L^2\)-boundedness altogether. We establish a global analogue of the Phong--Stein theory for quasi-homogeneous polynomial phases. We introduce a family of Newton polygons adapted to the regions near and away from the real zero curves of the Hessian, together with the corresponding box-area scales. The relative geometry of these Newton polygons and area scales characterizes global \(L^2\)-boundedness and determines the sharp \(L^2\)-estimates in the high- and low-frequency regimes. As an application, we determine the exact range of anisotropic homogeneous \(L^2\)-Sobolev estimates for the associated global Radon transform.

title: Emergence of large densities in a chemotaxis system with signal-dependent motility
abstract: In this paper, we focus on the emergence of large densities of a cell population in finite time in the following parabolic-elliptic Keller-Segel system with signal-dependent motility and a source term of logistic type \begin{equation} \begin{cases} u_{\varepsilon t} = Δ(e^{-v_\varepsilon}u_\varepsilon) + \varepsilon(κu_\varepsilon - μu_\varepsilon^2) ,\\ 0 =Δv_{\varepsilon}-v_\varepsilon+ u_{\varepsilon}. \end{cases} \end{equation} in a smooth bounded domain $Ω\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ with homogenuous Neumann boundary conditions and parameters $κ,μ>0$ and $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$. We will show that the solution $u_\varepsilon$ can exceed any certain value $M>0$ before a time $T(M)>0$ under the condition that $\varepsilon>0$ is sufficiently small. To prove the result, we show convergence of classical solutions of the first system to classical solutions of the corresponding limit system as $\varepsilon\searrow 0$ \begin{equation} \begin{cases} u_t=Δ(e^{-v}u),\\ -Δv+v=u. \end{cases} \end{equation} The main challenge is to find suitable bounds for $u_\varepsilon$ and $v_\varepsilon$, that are $\varepsilon$-independent, in Lebesgue and Hölder spaces, whereas for fixed $\varepsilon>0$ global existence and boundedness is known.

title: Self-gravitating Schrödinger--Poisson Solitons in Curved Spacetime
abstract: We formulate a description of self-gravitating Schrödinger--Poisson (SP) solitons in curved spacetime using a local inertial frame centered on the soliton. In the weak-field and non-relativistic regime, the effect of the background spacetime is incorporated into the SP equations through an effective tidal potential determined by the spacetime curvature. We apply this framework to a soliton moving along a circular equatorial geodesic around a Kerr black hole. The tidal field contains stationary and time-dependent quadrupolar components, which induce a deformation of the soliton and an associated mass quadrupole moment. We formulate the quadrupolar response in terms of the tidal deformability and the dimensionless Love number. We then estimate the gravitational radiation associated with the rotating deformed soliton and evaluate the corresponding characteristic strain for representative soliton sizes and orbital radii. A comparison with representative sensitivity curves of planned space-based gravitational-wave detectors identifies parameter regimes in which the estimated characteristic strain may lie within their sensitivity ranges. Our framework provides a systematic basis for investigating the tidal response of self-gravitating bosonic solitons in black-hole spacetimes and their potential gravitational-wave signatures.

title: The Kothe Radical in Novikov Algebras
abstract: We study the Kothe radical (the upper nil radical) in the variety of Novikov algebras. We prove that the class of weakly right nilpotent Novikov algebras coincides with the class of r-nil algebras and forms a radical class. We establish that the Kothe radical is a hereditary radical in the variety of Novikov algebras. Furthermore, we obtain a structural description of the Kothe radical as the intersection of ideals whose corresponding quotient algebras are prime K-semisimple algebras. Finally, we construct an example of a prime r-nil Novikov algebra over a field of characteristic p>0, which implies that the Baer radical is strictly contained in the Kothe radical in this case.

title: Nucleon decays into three leptons plus a kaon
abstract: We systematically investigate baryon-number-violating (BNV) nucleon decays into three leptons and a kaon within the framework of low-energy effective field theory (LEFT). We identify all kinematically allowed four-body decay modes involving a $K^+$ or $K^0$ meson and derive their decay widths induced by local dimension-9 operators in terms of the LEFT Wilson coefficients. These results are obtained by classifying the relevant operators, which contain three lepton and three quark fields, including one strange quark, according to their transformation properties under the chiral symmetry group, matching them onto chiral perturbation theory. By reanalyzing existing experimental data, we establish stringent bounds on the partial lifetimes of these four-body decay modes and derive corresponding constraints on the dimension-9 Wilson coefficients. Our results provide a convenient EFT framework for connecting the underlying BNV interactions to experimental searches for these exotic nucleon decays.

title: Maximum Energy of Integral Circulant Graphs with Same-Parity Exponents
abstract: The energy of a finite graph is the sum of the absolute values of the eigenvalues of its adjacency matrix. Let n be p to the power a times q to the power b, where p and q are distinct primes at least five and a and b, both positive integers, have the same parity. Among all nonempty sets D of proper divisors of n, the energy of the corresponding integral circulant graph is maximised by exactly two divisor sets: the divisors p to the power i times q to the power j with i plus j odd, and the divisors with i plus j even after removing p to the power a times q to the power b. We also determine the exact maximum energy. For the proof, weighted prime-power Ramanujan transforms yield an exact tensor-product representation of the graph energy, reducing the extremal problem to a weighted cut separating two prescribed vertices. After a sign conjugation, the relevant transforms decompose into embedded path blocks; the nontrivial blocks correspond to a weighted path together with chords of length three of weight negative one. We prove a sharp lower bound for cuts separating the two prescribed vertices in Kronecker products of these path blocks. For products of two such nontrivial blocks, equality holds only for cuts that isolate one of the two prescribed vertices. Combined with the energy-to-cut correspondence, these equality cases yield exactly the two maximising divisor sets.

title: Homological lifts of Arnold strangeness
abstract: We construct homological lifts of Arnold's strangeness $\operatorname{St}$ for long and closed plane curves. For long curves, we introduce a new $q$-variable quantization polynomial $\operatorname{St}_q$, an edge state sum, designed for categorification and construct a triply graded homology that recovers $\operatorname{St}_q$. We prove strictness by exhibiting long curves with the same number of crossings and the same $\operatorname{St}_q$ (in particular, the same rotation number and $\operatorname{St}$) that are distinguished by the homology. For closed curves, we introduce a corresponding new polynomial $\operatorname{St}_q$ and construct an edge homology. In this case $\operatorname{St}_q$ is recovered from a signed $q$-character $\operatorname{ch}_q$ defined on the canonical cycles of the homology rather than directly from a graded rank. Again, we exhibit closed curves with the same number of crossings and the same $\operatorname{St}_q$ (in particular, the same rotation number and $\operatorname{St}$) that are distinguished by the homology.

title: Silent Blindness: Fault Vulnerability of Hardware Malware Detectors
abstract: Hardware malware detectors (HMDs) classify hardware performance-counter measurements to identify malicious execution. Faults in their decision logic or parameters can weaken detection and allow malware to be classified as benign. We investigate this vulnerability through structural fault injection across a design space comprising 18 classifiers, four counter budgets, and AdaBoost and Bagging ensembles. The simulation evaluates 453,174 decision stuck-at and selected parameter bit-flip events on a 7,400-instance. Primary comparisons use 128 completed configurations. These completed-subset results are distinguished from the simulation summaries covering 140 configurations with enumerable fault sites. Fault outcomes are classified by their security consequences, including evasion, false-alarm increases, and metric silence. A fault is critical when malware recall decreases by at least five percentage points. Tree-based models exhibit a lower mean critical-fault fraction than function-based models, 5.3% versus 14.3%; exhaustive-only analysis preserves this ordering. Moreover, 72.3% of evaluated tree faults are metric-silent, changing both recall and false-positive rate by less than 0.1 percentage points without necessarily preserving individual predictions. Among the 27 completed matched comparisons, Bagging reduces criticality in 26, whereas AdaBoost increases it in two. Finally, an exact minimax selection method identifies protection candidates under additive unit costs and ideal correction. For a representative J48 detector, protecting 16 of 115 structural units reduces predicted maximum recall loss from 60.1 to 3.3 percentage points. These results characterize structural-model sensitivity and potential protection benefits; faulted RTL correspondence and physical hardening overhead remain unvalidated.

title: Structured Wavenumber-Domain Channel Estimation for LoS XL-MIMO
abstract: Near-field line-of-sight (LoS) channels in extremely large-scale multiple-input multiple-output (XL-MIMO) systems exhibit distinctive structural properties in the wavenumber domain. In this paper, we develop a structured wavenumber-domain channel estimation framework that first obtains an initial channel estimate using classical estimators and then refines it through a windowing-based refinement step that suppresses out-of-band noise by exploiting the localized spatial-frequency power distribution. The resulting estimate is subsequently enhanced through a convex constrained formulation that exploits the sparsity and low-rank structure of the wavenumber-domain channel. The corresponding sparsity and rank constraint bounds are selected using a conservative worst-case characterization over the relative position of the transmitter and receiver. Numerical results show that the proposed framework improves estimation accuracy, particularly at low signal-to-noise ratio, by effectively leveraging the structural properties of the wavenumber-domain channel.

title: Stationary Action Principles for Neuronal Growth
abstract: Neuronal growth is guided by biochemical, mechanical, and geometrical cues while being influenced by stochastic fluctuations in cytoskeletal dynamics, adhesion, and growth cone sensing. Here, we develop two complementary variational descriptions of mechanically guided axonal growth. First, for neurons growing on periodic parallel micropatterns, we use Langevin and Fokker--Planck models to derive a stochastic path action incorporating deterministic substrate guidance and random fluctuations. The probability of a growth trajectory decreases exponentially with this action, and the most probable trajectories correspond to minimum action paths for fixed boundary conditions. Second, for axons growing on substrates with spatially varying stiffness, we show that stiffness dependent traction generates mechanical guidance and axonal turning at stiffness interfaces. In the quasi-static limit, this response leads to a Fermat-like spatial action with an effective axonal refractive index determined by the traction and substrate stiffness relationship. The resulting framework predicts axonal refraction across stiffness boundaries, including an approximate Snell-like relation and a critical angle condition. Although the stochastic and Fermat-like actions have distinct physical meanings and ranges of validity, both describe how substrate mechanics constrain axonal trajectories. These results connect measurable quantities, including drift, diffusion, stiffness, traction, and growth direction, to global properties of axonal paths and provide a framework for designing biomimetic substrates for controlled neuronal growth and regeneration.

title: Pruning via Causal Attribution Preserves Reasoning Performance in Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at multi-step reasoning but incur substantial inference cost. We introduce Causal Attribution Pruning (CAP), a training-free method that identifies critical attention heads by measuring their causal impact on reasoning tasks and uses these head-level scores to guide fine-grained weight pruning. For each attention head, CAP estimates the expected performance degradation when the head is masked during forward passes on a small calibration set of reasoning problems. These causal scores are then converted into weight-level importance values for the corresponding projection matrices. Unlike magnitude-only or activation-based criteria, CAP's interventional measurement directly captures each head's functional contribution, yielding relative accuracy gains of up to 61% over Wanda on ARC-Challenge at 20% sparsity. We evaluate CAP on GSM8K, StrategyQA, and ARC-Challenge using Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct at 10%, 20%, and 50% sparsity. At moderate sparsity (10-20%), CAP improves over Wanda in most model-benchmark configurations. with especially large gains on ARC-Challenge for Llama-3. Our results suggest that attention-head-level causal attribution can better preserve reasoning performance on downstream benchmarks than correlational pruning criteria at equivalent sparsity, while remaining limited by coarse MLP attribution at 50% sparsity.

title: Automorphic functions for nilpotent extensions of curves over finite fields
abstract: We define and study the subspace of cuspidal functions for $G$-bundles (and its ramified analogs) on a class of nilpotent extensions of curves over a finite field. In the case of length $2$ extensions and of $G=\mathrm{GL}_2$, we prove that the space of cuspidal functions (for bundles with a fixed determinant) is finite-dimensional and provide bounds on its dimension. In this case we also relate cuspidality to Hecke finiteness, defined in terms of the action of some natural Hecke operators. Finally, we construct some Hecke eigenfunctions using the relation to Higgs bundles over the corresponding reduced curve.

title: Revenge of Monosemanticity: Neuron Specialization as a New Form of Feature Learning in MLPs
abstract: Understanding how neural networks learn and organize features is central to understanding their behavior. Much existing theory of feature learning has focused on the emergence of a global low-dimensional representation. We show that this picture is incomplete. In regression problems with clustered data, we demonstrate that multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) develop specialized neurons: individual neurons become strongly aligned with specific features relevant to a particular region of the input space. A substantial fraction of these neurons exhibit monosemanticity: they activate predominantly on inputs from the corresponding cluster. Thus, rather than learning a single global low-dimensional representation, MLPs learn a collection of local low-dimensional representations. Furthermore, we show that this ability to specialize gives MLPs a provable data-efficiency advantage over feature-learning methods based on a global low-dimensional representation.

title: Semisimple module categories with fusion rules of the compact flag manifold type
abstract: We classify semisimple left module categories over the representation category of a type A quantum group whose fusion rules arise from Levi subalgebras. The classification is connected to equivariant Poisson structures on compact flag manifolds in the operator-algebraic setting, and on semisimple coadjoint orbits in the algebraic setting. We also provide an explicit construction based on the BGG categories of deformed quantum enveloping algebras, whose unitarizability corresponds to being of quotient type. Finally, we present a brief discussion of the non-quantum group case

title: Role-Augmented Intent-Driven Generative Search Engine Optimization
abstract: Generative search engines (GSEs), which combine large language models (LLMs) with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), are reshaping how users access Web information and making source visibility and influence in generated responses new optimization objectives. Existing generative search engine optimization (G-SEO) methods seek to improve content visibility, but many rely on direct access to target queries or GSE feedback elicited by those queries. However, Web content is typically optimized and published before future user queries are known, making G-SEO without access to target queries or their associated feedback an important yet underexplored problem. To address this, we propose RAID, a Role-Augmented Intent-Driven G-SEO method that operates without access to target queries or query-dependent GSE feedback. RAID infers a primary retrieval intent from source content, refines it through 4W multi-role deep reflection on prospective searchers' information needs, and uses both the primary and refined intents to jointly plan and rewrite source content. We further extend GEO-BENCH with diverse topic-related query variants, using both the original queries and their variants exclusively for evaluation to assess generalization to queries unseen during optimization. Across 100 samples and 500 evaluation queries, RAID achieves Relative Improvement Scores (RIS) of 3.00\% for Objective Overall and 1.32\% for Subjective Average, exceeding the best corresponding results among the nine predefined GEO rewriting strategies by 1.31 and 0.74 percentage points, respectively. With an optimization considered effective when $\mathrm{RIS}>0$, its effective optimization rates for Objective Overall and Subjective Average average 58.0\%, exceeding the highest corresponding average among the predefined strategies by 4.5 percentage points.

title: On quaternionic analysis and a certain generalized fractal-fractional $ψ$-Fueter operator
abstract: This paper introduces a fractal $ψ$-Fueter operator in the quaternionic context inspired by the concepts of proportional derivative and Hausdorff derivative ({fractal derivative}) of a function with respect to a fractal measure. Moreover, we establish the corresponding Stokes and Borel-Pompeiu formulas associated to this generalized fractal $ψ$-Fueter operator with respect to a vector valued function induced by truncated exponential functions.

title: Optimizing Evolution Under Cyclic Selection: the Case of B Cells
abstract: Rapid evolutionary adaptation may be necessary for organisms facing strong environmental pressures. Although selection often acts continuously, in the case of B cells evolving high affinity antibodies in germinal centers, selection can take place after multiple rounds of division. To study how the number of divisions between selection events affects adaptation, we develop a minimal computational model of cyclic selection. We find that the optimal average mutation rate per division and the corresponding adaptation velocity are nearly invariant across number of divisions between selections, and we quantitatively explain this behavior with a theory based on the dynamics of the "nose", i.e. the fittest individuals in the population. We also find that when the number of divisions between selection events is large, then mutating every division results in slower adaptation than mutating only at the last division before selection (as is the case for B cells). Our model provides a framework for understanding adaptation in natural and experimental systems subject to cyclic selection.

title: Neuronal Identity as an Organizational Basis for Analyzing Neural Population Dynamics
abstract: Individual neurons exhibit diverse molecular, morphological, and electrophysiological properties that shape their distinct roles in neural circuits. While these multimodal features are largely shared across individuals, they remain an underutilized source of information in analyzing neural population dynamics. We posit that these shared biological profiles provide a common reference for relating neural dynamics across subjects and recording sessions. Our framework leverages this structure by routing neurons into latent groups based on their biological profiles and analyzing population dynamics through group-level representations. Because these assignments are anchored in biological properties that are consistent across subjects, the learned organization supports transfer to unseen animals without retraining or neuron-wise correspondence. We evaluate our framework on whole-brain calcium imaging in larval zebrafish and large-scale electrophysiology in the mouse visual cortex. Across both species and recording modalities, the framework delivers state-of-the-art performance in both neural decoding and manifold analysis: it achieves superior decoding of behavior and stimulus labels while better preserving the temporal consistency and local geometric structure of latent trajectories on unseen data. Our experiments demonstrate that not only does providing biological features improve baseline performance, but our proposed framework achieves even stronger results by using these properties to explicitly structure the population rather than treating them as auxiliary inputs. Together, these results suggest that organizing neural populations by their multimodal biological features offers a promising framework for generalizing population dynamics across subjects and recording sessions.

title: Advantage of Sample Complexity in Quantum PAC Learning Requires Inverse Access to State-Preparation Unitaries
abstract: Whether quantum computation can reduce the amount of data required for conventional machine learning is a central problem in quantum machine learning. In probably approximately correct (PAC) learning, a learner receives training examples sampled from an unknown probability distribution. Quantum PAC learning extends this framework by allowing access to quantum examples, which are quantum states that coherently encode this distribution, or to unitaries that prepare quantum examples, with or without inverse access. When only copies of quantum examples are available, the optimal worst-case sample complexity asymptotically matches that of classical learning. In contrast, access to both a preparation unitary and its inverse can improve the accuracy dependence of query complexity. However, it has remained open whether access to the preparation unitary alone suffices for this improvement. In this work, we resolve this question by determining the optimal query complexity with forward-only access, taking the worst case over compatible preparation unitaries and their dimensions. In both realizable and agnostic PAC learning, this complexity matches, up to constant factors, the optimal sample complexity achievable with classical examples or copies of quantum examples. To prove these results, we construct, for any algorithm with forward-only access, a simulator that approximates the algorithm's Haar-averaged output state using as many copies of the prepared state as the algorithm makes queries. These results show that inverse access is essential for the known improvement in accuracy dependence in this worst-case setting. Beyond PAC learning, our reduction provides a general tool for transferring lower bounds for state copies to query lower bounds for forward-only access to the corresponding preparation unitaries.

title: Asymptotics and finite sample bounds for prediction and smoothing in Wright-Fisher hidden Markov models
abstract: We study signal prediction and smoothing in hidden Markov models whose latent signal is a multi-type Wright-Fisher diffusion and whose discrete-time observations are categorical. We consider a repeated-sampling regime with finitely many inspection times and large within-time samples. Under neutrality and parent-independent mutation, the Bayesian predictive and smoothing laws admit exact representations as mixtures of Dirichlet distributions. We show that the one-step predictive and local smoothing laws converge in total variation to the corresponding Wright-Fisher transition and bridge laws determined by the neighboring population frequencies, thereby justifying plug-in approximations based on empirical proportions. For prediction, we derive explicit finite-sample bounds for this approximation and for bounded predictive functionals such as diversity, together with a finite-sample concentration bound for the marginal smoother. The joint posterior at the inspection times concentrates at the target frequencies and satisfies a Bernstein-von Mises limit with distinct interior and boundary regimes, with Gaussian and Gamma limits on different scales. The results allow arbitrary dependence across inspection times. A key technical ingredient is a fixed-interval tail bound for the coalescent-based dual death process.

title: Intercomponent vortex interaction and dynamics in a uniform Bose quantum liquid
abstract: We investigate the interaction and dynamics of vortices belonging to different components of a binary uniform quantum liquid. Using the coupled extended Gross-Pitaevskii equations with logarithmic beyond-mean-field corrections, we derive the asymptotic interaction potential between well-separated vortices. The interaction potential retains the asymptotic form $s^{-2}$ as a function of the intervortex distance s, but its coefficient depends on the background density through the quantum fluctuation. As a result, the interaction between vortices changes from attractive to repulsive at a critical density. Real-time simulations demonstrate a corresponding reversal of orbital motion of a vortex pair from clockwise to counterclockwise, consistent with their Magnus response.

title: A geometric--analytic proof of the reverse isoperimetric inequality in Einstein gravity
abstract: We develop a geometric--analytic proof of the reverse isoperimetric inequality for compact AdS black hole horizons in Einstein gravity. At fixed thermodynamic volume, a York slice/Jacobi variation of the gravitational action shows that the spherical Schwarzschild--AdS solution is a strict local entropy maximum against generic non-spherical deformations. The finite global extension is formulated within the hypotheses of the Sherif--Dunsby (SD) rigidity theorem: compactness and spherical topology, the required intrinsic Ricci decomposition $\mathrm{Ric}_h=α\,\mathbf e\!\otimes\!\mathbf e+βN$ with $α\neqβ$, a proper conformal transformation of the hypersurface metric given by $\widetilde h_{ab}=e^{2\varphi}h_{ab}$ that preserves its intrinsic scalar curvature, $\widetilde R\equiv R[\widetilde h]=R[h]\equiv R>0$, and negative sheet expansion. Compactness and $S^3$ topology are built into the class considered here. In the static spherical sector such as Schwarzschild--AdS and RN--AdS, the SD Ricci form is naturally realized while it is an additional restriction for Kerr--AdS case. For the $S^3$ topology, a positive Yamabe type conformal class exists for which the Yamabe theorem provides a representative of positive and constant scalar-curvature. We further restrict to the scalar-curvature preserving conformal transformation required by the SD theorem. The negative sheet expansion is obtained using gravitational focusing. Within this admissible class, a non-round Kerr--AdS horizon cannot maximize the entropy, while fixed thermodynamic volume selects the corresponding round Schwarzschild--AdS comparator. The analysis thus establishes a generic local entropy maximum and a finite global result within the stated geometric rigidity class, identifying the role of gravity in reversing the ordinary isoperimetric problem.

title: Bridgeland stability and Gieseker stability I: Limit stability
abstract: We study the large volume limit of Bridgeland stability conditions on smooth projective varieties. For each fixed ray in a suitable angular sector, we prove that an object of $\mathrm{D}^b(X)$ is Bridgeland (semi)stable in the corresponding hearts for all sufficiently large radii if and only if it is a pure $H$-Gieseker (semi)stable sheaf. In this sector, we identify the category of coherent sheaves as the limiting heart in the sense of eventual membership. We also identify a perverse coherent limiting heart in the opposite angular sector. The key ingredients are uniform HN-phase estimates for bounded families of pure sheaves, coefficient bounds for the coherent images of potential destabilizers, and a criterion forcing narrow exact sequences in the varying hearts to be bounded saturated coherent sequences.

title: Prussian blue and Prussian white thin-film electrodes: Single-step electrodeposition for anode and cathode applications
abstract: This study examines how deposition potential influences the composition and nanoscale structure of Prussian Blue (PB)/Prussian White (PW)-family films, providing an experimental basis for assessing their proposed functions. Films were grown directly on Au/Cr/Si in a single potentiostatic step from a common aqueous bath at $-0.20$ to $+0.40$\,V versus a saturated calomel electrode, with a fixed deposition charge of 10\,mC. Electron microscopy, elemental analysis, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and Raman spectroscopy revealed potential-dependent chemistry and nonmonotonic morphology. EDS indicated greater K incorporation in lower-potential deposits, whose Fe~2p and Raman features were consistent with more reduced, PW-like environments. Surface K/Fe ratios varied nonmonotonically from 1.129 to 1.322 across the series, corresponding to 52.95--56.94\% K within the detected K+Fe population. Larger faceted crystallites at $+0.30$\,V contrasted with finer pyramids and cracks at $+0.40$\,V. Selected PB-like and PW-like regions had local cubic lattice parameters of $(10.31\pm0.10)$\,Å and $(10.36\pm0.10)$\,Å, respectively; their overlapping uncertainties prevent discrimination by lattice spacing alone. Cross-sectional maps showed broadly uniform framework-element distributions within locally continuous coatings. Together, these observations relate deposition conditions to contrasting chemical and morphological starting states without establishing bulk stoichiometry or phase purity. A literature-grounded outlook identifies ion storage, sensing, electrochromism, resistive switching, and ion handling as research opportunities requiring functional validation in these films.

title: Non-linear effects in coherent photoproduction of heavy quarkonia off nuclei: Green's function formalism vs Balitsky-Kovchegov equation
abstract: We present an analysis of QCD non-linear (NL) effects in the coherent photoproduction of charmonia off nuclei at high energies corresponding to future measurements at the LHC. For the first time, we confront the energy evolution of such effects within our rigorous Green's function (GF) formalism with results from Refs.~\cite{Cepila:2025ujv,Cepila:2024qge}, which are based on the solution of the leading-order (LO) and next-to-leading-order (NLO) Balitsky-Kovchegov (BK) evolution equations. We demonstrate a huge difference in the NL effects between these two formalisms, exhibiting a rather strong rise with photon energy. Our analysis shows that NLO calculations of the BK equation from Ref.~\cite{Cepila:2024qge} slow down the rate of the high-energy LO evolution of NL effects. Although these calculations reduce the differences between the GF and BK predictions, they still lead to a much stronger onset of leading-twist shadowing effects compared to the GF formalism. The BK equation in its present form cannot be applied to nuclear targets and thus requires a non-trivial modification that properly incorporates quantum coherence effects.

title: Residual dynamics determine dissipation in strongly coupled linear Langevin systems
abstract: Interactions shape the properties of many physical and biological nonequilibrium systems, but whether collective operation raises or lowers entropy production remains difficult to predict. Here, we show that strong coupling suppresses irreversible circulation associated with the directly coupled degrees of freedom. In identical two-dimensional systems, this suppression is monotonic for nonzero coupling modes and guarantees a monotonic decrease of the entropy production rate (EPR), with the corresponding probability currents vanishing in the strong-coupling limit. In higher dimensions, suppressing the circulation associated with the coupled degrees of freedom does not generally eliminate all irreversible circulation, since the remaining degrees of freedom can still sustain nonequilibrium currents. The EPR of these residual dynamics sets the strong-coupling limit, providing a criterion for whether a given choice of coupled variables leads to lower dissipation than the uncoupled system. The approach to this limit depends on how the finite-coupling current correction aligns with the residual current. Further, we show that convergence to residual dynamics in the strong-coupling limit also applies to coupled non-identical systems. Finally, we demonstrate the predicted EPR reduction in nonlinear models of vertebrate hair-cell bundles and bacterial chemotaxis.

title: Calculation of distant retrograde orbits and their use in space weather forecasting
abstract: There is current renewed interest in using Sun-Earth distant retrograde orbits (DROs) for a space weather forecasting mission, which would temporarily place spacecraft at a position near the Sun-Earth line, but closer to the Sun than the L1 point (such as the ESA HENON mission and ESA SHIELD concept). With in situ observations of the magnetic field on a DRO, the southward ($B_z < 0$) magnetic field of interplanetary coronal mass ejections (ICMEs), which is not routinely accessible remotely, could be measured several hours in advance. This $B_z < 0$ field is a decisive factor for forecasting geomagnetic storm intensity. We present an analysis of DROs at different sub-L1 distances for their efficacy for a space weather forecasting mission. An open-source numerical framework to generate DRO trajectories is presented. Our pre-calculated orbits in Heliocentric Earth Ecliptic coordinates can be introduced into numerical or empirical simulations of the ambient solar wind and ICMEs. We then analyze the corresponding forecast lead times, the resulting observational gaps depending on the number of spacecraft and distance of a DRO, and the "cone of acceptance" of the maximum longitudinal separation of a spacecraft to the Sun-Earth line. We define different domains regarding radial evolution and longitudinal CME structure, and show the historical coverage of sub-L1 ICME observations with our ICMECAT catalog. An optimal mission configuration can be selected based on the characteristics of DROs presented here, depending on the requirements of such a mission deemed acceptable with respect to results on CME evolution and coherence.

title: The Lifecycle and Emission Properties of PAHs in Cosmological Hydrodynamic Galaxy Formation Simulations
abstract: We present the first cosmological model for the lifecycle and luminous properties of PAHs in galaxies as they evolve from z=6-->0. We model 40 zoom-in galaxies, coupled with an on-the-fly model for the evolution of dust grains in the ISM. We approximate PAHs as ultrasmall (a < 13 Angstrom) carbonaceous dust grains, and couple this model with single-photon excitation calculations to compute the emergent mid-infrared spectra. (1) If we assume that dust is large upon formation, then PAHs are naturally able to form in situ in the ISM via grain-grain shattering. Interstellar collision velocities increase in low density, diffuse gas in our model; as galaxies evolve, the increase in fractional mass of diffuse gas drives an increase in grain-grain collision velocities and a corresponding rise in the PAH mass fraction (qPAH) from ~5 x 10^{-4} at z~4 to ~10^{-2} at z~0. (2) Increased PAH production in the diffuse ISM results in an inverse relationship between qPAH and the molecular gas fraction. (3) The PAH light-to-mass ratio scales linearly with the radiation field intensity (LPAH/MPAH ~ G_0) but anti-correlates with qPAH, because high-Sigma_SFR galaxies have a denser ISM that suppresses shattering. This means the physical qPAH and observed LPAH/LFIR do not evolve in lockstep. (4) The PAH-metallicity relationship (PZR) arises naturally in this framework: galaxies enrich and grow their diffuse ISM fraction simultaneously, linking rising metallicity to rising qPAH. Our models represent the first to reproduce the PZR observed across z=0-2. (5) The LPAH-SFR and LPAH-M_mol relations emerge from two effects: more massive galaxies have larger PAH reservoirs, and higher-SFR galaxies excite their PAHs more efficiently per unit mass. Taken together, these results suggest that grain-grain shattering in the diffuse ISM is the main driver behind the evolution of cosmic PAH abundances.

title: Benchmarking quantum-annealing-based approaches for factory layout planning
abstract: The earlystage of factory layout planning has a direct effect on the operating costs, efficiency, and productivity of manufacturing systems. Conventional automated planning approaches often face a trade-off between solution quality and computational effort. Recent studies have investigated the potential of quantum annealing (QA) for solving factory layout planning problems. However, existing studies have mainly focused on individual QA-based formulations, whereas current hybrid QA solvers support multiple model types that combine QA and classical methods. To explore the potential of QA for factory layout planning, this paper benchmarks four QA based approaches implemented with the corresponding solvers, including an iterative binary quadratic model (IBQM), a hybrid discrete quadratic model (HDQM), a hybrid constrained quadratic model (HCQM), and a hybrid nonlinear model (HNLM). To improve scalability, an iterative decomposition strategy is developed for IBQM, while a candidate selection procedure is introduced for HDQM. The approaches are benchmarked against genetic algorithm, particle swarm optimization, and a hybrid tabu search and simulated annealing approach on 14 layout instances with different layout sizes, geometric complexity, spatial restrictions, and transport route configurations. The comparative analysis considers solution quality, computation time, and scalability. The results show that QA-based approaches achieve competitive solution quality and substantial computational advantages, reducing computation time by up to 94.51% relative to the classical reference methods. Among them, IBQM obtains the best solution quality in 78.6% of the instances, with a maximum improvement of 17.41% associated with an 81.34% reduction in computation time. These findings provide a basis for their further application in industrial layout planning.

title: Information-theoretic entropy imaging of quantum matter
abstract: Phase transitions can generate intricate spatial organization invisible to spatially averaged probes, yet quantitative measures of this organization remain limited. Here we develop "entropy imaging," an information-theoretic technique that harnesses lossless compression to quantify spatial complexity, predictability, and order in quantum materials. Using this approach, emergent spatial textures can be imaged and converted into an experimentally-accessible observable: the computable information density (CID), a compression-based measure of information complexity that approaches the Shannon entropy rate in the large-system limit. Applied to millikelvin microwave impedance microscopy of graphene, the method reveals a pronounced maximum in the CID near quantum Hall transitions, a quantitative measure of the information-rich spatial organization of the critical landscape. A disordered Hofstadter model reproduces this behavior and shows that the CID can identify the quantum critical point from a sequence of images, without ensemble averaging over disorder realizations. The same framework tracks fractional quantum Hall transitions and resolves isolated fractional puddles that coexist with a disordered background. By contrast, the trivial band-edge crossover in a MoSe2/WS2 moiré heterobilayer exhibits qualitatively different behavior, suggesting that the pronounced CID enhancement observed at the quantum Hall critical point is not simply a generic feature of a conductive-insulating crossover. We further show that the geometric information encoded in CID is not reducible to a correlation length, and it can even distinguish spatial textures with identical multifractal statistics. Together, these results establish lossless compression as a framework for quantifying emergent spatial organization in quantum materials, with portability across imaging modalities and physical systems.

title: The Proof-Theoretic Foundations of the Principle of Reiteration in Natural Deduction
abstract: This paper investigates the proof-theoretic foundations of the principle of reiteration (R) in natural deduction, arguing that its legitimacy originates in the structural preservation of formulae within sequent calculus rather than in an independent logical rule. By examining singlesuccedent and multisuccedent sequent calculus, we demonstrate how logical operations transform principal formulae while preserving unaffected antecedent and succedent contexts. We subsequently analyse the schematic formulation of reiteration and compare natural deduction derivations with corresponding sequent calculus derivations. This comparison identifies two fundamental functions of reiteration, namely the reuse of previously employed formulae and the restoration of previously derived conclusions. We conclude that reiteration introduces no independent inferential content but explicitly represents the structural continuity of inferential dependencies already included into sequent calculus.

title: A new gradient-free active subspace estimation method with application to rare event probability estimation
abstract: To reduce the cost of estimating the probability of a rare event involving a very large number of random parameters, we propose a new strategy for dimension reduction coupled with a surrogate model for the expensive part of the algorithm. To this end, we extend the Ordinary Kriging Active Subspace (OK-AS) method into a sequential version. Our approach consists of iteratively re-estimating the active subspace using a Kriging surrogate trained in a rotated coordinate system until the active subspace stabilises. This method allows for a reduction in prediction error and a better approximation of the active subspace on a benchmark of test problems. Furthermore, we integrate our algorithm into an efficient pre-existing approach for estimating the probability of a rare event. This approach is based on learning the active subspace associated with the random event whose probability is to be estimated. The sequential learning of an importance sampling density is necessary and corresponds to the expensive part of this strategy. To circumvent this issue, we integrate our sequential OK-AS version into the estimation of the importance sampling density. The numerical results indicate that our method allows for reducing the cost required to obtain a precise estimate of the rare event probability.

title: On the Complexity of Computing Outputs of a Metric Turing Machine
abstract: The classes MidP, MedP, and $\small{\overline{\text{MedP}}}$ contain functions that compute the median solution for certain types of problems. In this paper, for these classes we introduce analogous classes of functions that compute the k-th solution, where k is an order function that depends on the input. We prove that the classes MidP, MedP, and $\small{\overline{\text{MedP}}}$ are polynomial-time 1-Turing inter-reducible with the corresponding classes, where the order function is from FP or FP$^{\text{#P}}$. For MedP we also prove that it coincides with the corresponding classes, where the order function is from FP or #P. For several inclusions between function classes we give equivalent inclusions between language classes. In particular, we establish inclusion relations between MaxP and median classes MidP, MedP, and $\small{\overline{\text{MedP}}}$. We also prove that NPSV$_{\text{t}} \subseteq$ MaxP $\subseteq$ FP$^{\text{NP}}$ and both inclusions are proper if and only if NP $\neq$ coNP.

title: Matchings and shape-Wilf-Equivalence of sets of patterns of length three I: Triples
abstract: Permutation pattern avoidance on Ferrers boards has become a central topic in enumerative combinatorics with important connections to matchings, set partitions, and other combinatorial structures as it allows one to build families of Wilf-equivalent patterns. While shape-Wilf-equivalence classes have been completely determined for individual patterns and pairs of patterns of length three, the corresponding classification for larger pattern sets has remained open. In this paper, we provide a complete classification of the shape-Wilf-equivalence classes of triples of patterns of length three. Our proofs use a bijective encoding of pattern avoiding transversals to establish all equivalence classes. As an application, we enumerate matchings avoiding triples of patterns of length three for all, extending previous results of Bloom and Elizalde. These enumerative results identify additional families of combinatorial objects counted by the Fuss-Catalan numbers and by other integer sequences appearing in the OEIS.

title: Functional second-order Gaussian Poincaré inequalities
abstract: In this paper, we work in the framework of Hilbert-valued Wiener structures and derive a functional version of the second-order Gaussian Poincaré inequality that leads to abstract bounds for Gaussian process approximation in $d_2$ distance used by Bourguin and Campese (Electron. J. Probab., 2020). As pointed out by Bassetti, Bourguin, Campese, and Peccati (Statist. Probab. Lett., 2026) this distance alone does not imply weak convergence in infinite dimensions, we also consider $d_2^\dagger$, obtained by adding the absolute difference of the second moments. This metric metrizes $2$-Wasserstein convergence and agrees with $d_2$ for centered variables with matching covariance operators. Our abstract bounds are flexible and can be applied in various examples including functional Breuer-Major central limit theorems, shallow neural networks, and spatial statistics of SPDE solutions. In these applications, the covariance estimates also give the second-moment convergence needed for weak convergence in the corresponding Hilbert spaces.

title: Orientifold and Integrability: $\mathcal{N}=4$ Super-Yang-Mills on $\mathbb{RP}^4$
abstract: We study planar $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory (SYM) on the real projective space $\mathbb{RP}^4$ using integrability, holography and supersymmetric localization, and discuss its relation to orientifolds in string theory. We show that the integrability of $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM is preserved when combining the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ involution defining $\mathbb{RP}^4$ with the action of the charge conjugation of the SU$(N)$ gauge group. We demonstrate this by calculating one-point functions of non-BPS single-trace operators in various subsectors at weak coupling, which can be mapped to overlaps between energy eigenstates and crosscap states in integrable spin chains. The results exhibit a parity selection rule, a hallmark of integrability, and are given in terms of a ratio of determinants. Building on these results, we conjecture a closed formula for general single-trace operators. We further provide evidence that this construction is holographically dual to a probe orientifold O1-plane in $\text{AdS}_5\times \text{S}^5$ by constructing the corresponding worldsheet crosscap states in the pp-wave limit. Finally, we use supersymmetric localization to compute one-point functions of half-BPS operators exactly at finite $g_{\rm YM}$ and $N$. The computation reduces to two-dimensional Yang-Mills theory on $\mathbb{RP}^2$ twisted by charge conjugation and leads to a matrix integral of a Wishart-Laguerre type. In the planar limit, the exact result interpolates between the weak-coupling gauge-theory result, the strong-coupling supergravity prediction for the orientifold, and the worldsheet crosscap in the pp-wave limit.

title: Critical Diameters and Vietoris-Rips Filtrations
abstract: We relate critical diameters of finite configurations to the topology of Vietoris-Rips complexes.
